hero.body:
A former Treasure Coast Hospice employee was arrested after Stuart police say she stole two rings from a deceased patient and pawned one of them in Port St. Lucie. Latoya Morrine Moye of Fort Pierce faces a third-degree grand theft charge in connection with the theft.

 Stuart Police Department officers received a report on Aug. 18 that two rings were missing from a deceased Treasure Coast Hospice patient. A detective searched pawn transaction records and discovered that Moye had pawned a ring in Port St. Lucie one day after it was reported missing. The ring was recovered, and the patient's family identified it as one of the two missing rings.

 Pawn records and surveillance video identified Moye as the person who made the transaction, according to Stuart police. A warrant was issued for her arrest, and she was later arrested in St. Lucie County.

 The second ring remains missing. Treasure Coast Hospice is covering the cost of retrieving the recovered ring and returning it to the family.

hero.body:
Port St. Lucie homeowners are finding flyers in their mailboxes explaining how the city's $24 million settlement with its former trash hauler will show up on their property tax bill. The settlement is being distributed over 95,000 eligible properties, with about 57,000 homeowners who have stayed at the same property since the 2022 tax roll receiving an estimated $364 credit and roughly 38,000 other eligible properties, including newer properties added to the tax roll and those approved through an eligibility claims process, receiving an estimated $64 credit. The notices are arriving at the same time property owners across St. Lucie County are receiving their TRIM notices, the annual estimate of what they can expect to owe in property taxes.

The credits are the result of the city's lawsuit against Waste Pro, the company Port St. Lucie sued after two years of unreliable service and missed pickups. The two sides settled in April for $24 million, days before the case was set to go to trial. In June, the City Council voted to return all of that money to residents through property tax credits rather than mailing checks.

The decision to issue credits instead of checks drew loud objections at the June meeting. Residents told the council they wanted cash in hand. Only Councilwoman Jolien Caraballo supported that approach. Other council members raised concerns about the cost of printing and mailing tens of thousands of checks and the chance that payments could be lost or stolen. When the final vote was taken, boos and jeers came from the audience.

Council members also agreed that none of the settlement money would be moved into the city's general fund. Councilman Anthony Bonna said it's the taxpayers' money and the taxpayers were the ones who were wronged. The city's current trash hauler is FCC Environmental Services. Residents have continued pressing the city over once-a-week pickup, and the council considered whether settlement money could pay for a second weekly collection day before rejecting that option, saying it would only work until the money ran out. Voters are expected to weigh in on twice-weekly pickup through a straw ballot question in November.

Port St. Lucie homeowners are finding flyers in their mailboxes explaining how the city's $24 million settlement with Waste Pro will appear as credits on their property tax bills. The settlement money is being distributed over 95,000 eligible properties following the city's lawsuit against its former trash hauler for two years of unreliable service and missed pickups.

About 57,000 homeowners who have stayed at the same property since the 2022 tax roll will receive an estimated $364 credit. Roughly 38,000 other eligible properties, including newer properties added to the tax roll and those approved through an eligibility claims process, will receive an estimated $64 credit. The two sides settled in April for $24 million, days before the case was set to go to trial.

The City Council voted in June to return all of the settlement money to residents through property tax credits rather than mailing checks. The decision drew loud objections at the June meeting, with residents telling the council they wanted cash in hand. Only Councilwoman Jolien Caraballo supported that approach. Other council members raised concerns about the cost of printing and mailing tens of thousands of checks and the chance that payments could be lost or stolen. When the final vote was taken, boos and jeers came from the audience.

The credits are landing as property owners across St. Lucie County are receiving their TRIM notices, the annual estimate of what they can expect to owe in property taxes. Council members agreed that none of the settlement money would be moved into the city's general fund. Councilman Anthony Bonna said it's the taxpayers' money and the taxpayers were the ones who were wronged. Port St. Lucie's current trash hauler is FCC Environmental Services. Voters are expected to weigh in on twice-weekly pickup through a straw ballot question in November.
